subject: compound-interest
title: The Math of Compounding
summary: Exponential growth, the Rule of 72, and why time beats timing.

cards.title: The pizza question
cards.text: Skip a $2 slice of pizza every day for a year and you save $730. Invest it at 5% and leave it alone. How much do you think it becomes after 30 years?

cards.title: The formula
cards.text: Compound growth multiplies instead of adds: amount = start × (1 + rate)^years. At 5%, $100 becomes $105, then $110.25. In year two, you earn 25 cents on your first $5 of interest.
cards.example: The pizza answer: $730 grows to $931.69 after 5 years and $3,155.02 after 30 years, with nothing added.

cards.title: The Rule of 72
cards.text: To estimate how long money takes to double, divide 72 by the yearly rate. At 9%, money doubles in about 72 ÷ 9 = 8 years. At 6%, about 12 years.
cards.example: It is a shortcut, not exact, but it is close for normal rates.

cards.title: Why the end matters most
cards.text: Because growth multiplies, most of the dollar gain comes late. $100 at 5% gains about $63 in the first 10 years but about $176 in the next 15.

cards.title: A careful analogy
cards.text: People say practicing 1% better each day compounds: 1.01³⁶⁵ ≈ 37.8. That is real math, but skills don't grow that neatly. Progress in golf or soccer comes in bumps and plateaus. The useful lesson: consistency over long periods beats short bursts.

cards.question: If compounding rewards time so much, why don't more people start saving early? What gets in the way?
nudges: Think about what is easy to see now vs. later.
Would you rather have $730 of pizza or $3,155 thirty years from now? Why?

questions.q: Using the Rule of 72, how long does money take to double at 6%?
$100 at 5%: how much does it gain in year 2?

options.why: 5% of $105 = $5.25. The extra 25 cents is interest on interest.
That is simple interest. Compounding earns on the $105.
That is the total gain over both years.

questions.q: Why does most of the gain come in later years?

options.text: Each year's growth is a percent of a bigger balance.
options.why: Right. Multiplying a bigger number gives a bigger jump.

options.text: Banks raise the rate over time.
options.why: Even at a fixed rate, the dollar gains grow.
Not the reason. It is the math of multiplying.
